source.title: Mixture Data for Training Cannot Ensure Out-of-distribution Generalization
source.authors: Song-Ming Zhang; Yu-Xiao Luo; Qi-Zhou Wang; Hao-Ang Chi; Xiao-Feng Chen; Bo Han; Jin-Yan Li

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests image-classification generalization error as training sample size changes and reports both power-law declines and non-decreasing or non-monotonic trends. This refines or challenges extending scaling-law behavior to image settings, but it does not test language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The reported outcomes are OOD classification generalization errors versus training sample size, not held-out language-model pretraining loss. The paper does not fit or compare scaling exponents, test parameter-count or compute scaling, or test compute-optimal allocations. Results cited from other work are not recorded. Hyperparameter optimization and algorithm comparisons without a training-size scaling result are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains small image classifiers on growing training sets and plots OOD test error against sample size. It explicitly sets this against the neural scaling law (Kaplan et al.). It reports power-law decline in some shifts and flat or non-monotonic curves in others. This bears on V5 (image modality, transfer to shifted distributions). It does not bear on language-model pretraining loss, compute allocation, shape or downstream predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors add a theoretical account: targets inside the convex hull of the training mixture get a tighter error bound, while targets outside it do not. On that basis, more mixed training data cannot guarantee OOD improvement.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses image-classification networks and OOD classification error over training sample-size sweeps; it does not use the language-model pretraining-loss scaling setup or test parameter/token/compute scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported error trends vary with target distribution and shift severity, including rotation angle, blur level, task pair, and dataset/domain.
record.problems: The evidence concerns image-classification OOD error rather than language-model held-out pretraining loss. The relevant curve values are presented only in figures, and the text does not report fitted exponents or power-law fit statistics. The experiments use a limited set of datasets and architectures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were included for hyperparameter optimization, DomainBed algorithm comparisons, or the proposed data-selection method because their reported outcomes do not test the scaling behavior named by the versions. Cited results from other work were also excluded.

untested.parts: Scaling with parameters or compute; in-distribution test loss; explicit power-law fits or exponents; video and other modalities; repeated data; scale beyond tiny CNNs and WRNs trained on small binary or few-class subsets.
All: no extrapolation from fitted laws.
All: architecture shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
All: no exponents are fitted or compared.

missing.what: OOD error versus training size N after ImageNet pre-training then fine-tuning, and with augmentation. Pre-trained WRN-10-2 error 'still rises' for the 135° target. This bears on V5's transfer/fine-tuning regime.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is weak for scaling-law purposes. All curves are figure-only, with no fitted exponents and no numeric values. The models are tiny (0.12M-parameter SmallConv, WRN-10-2, WRN-16-4), the tasks are mostly binary, and only training-set size varies. The measure is OOD classification error, not in-distribution loss, so the results speak to V5's transfer reading rather than the core power law. Fig. 4 varies the OOD evaluation-set size M, not training data, so it is correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their growth with compute.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.

The paper measures OOD image-classification generalization error versus training sample size, not held-out pretraining loss; it does not test video, repeated-data training, or language-model transfer.
Predictability of downstream task performance from model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, parameter counting, or training schedules.
